summary: Records the text of the Memorandum of Understanding between the IETF and ICANN about the technical work of the Internet Assigned Numbers Authority, signed on March 1, 2000 and ratified by the ICANN Board on March 10, 2000. It is an informational memo.

eli5.summary: This is a written agreement between two groups about who does what in keeping the Internet's lists of numbers and names.

subtitle: The written agreement that says how IANA does protocol parameter work for the IETF.

tldr.problem: The IANA technical team had become part of ICANN, so the IETF and ICANN needed a clear agreement on how protocol parameter assignments would be made.
tldr.mechanism: A Memorandum of Understanding says IANA assigns parameters only as RFCs direct, takes technical guidance from the IESG, and appeals go to the IESG and then the IAB.
tldr.outcome: The RFC puts the MoU signed on March 1, 2000 on record. Domain name and IP address block policy is left outside its scope.

today: RFC 2860 is an Informational document, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It preserves the text of the MoU as signed in March 2000.

sections.title: What the MoU Is and Who Signed It
sections.content:
RFC 2860 is an Informational document that records the text of a Memorandum of Understanding between the IETF and ICANN concerning the technical work of the Internet Assigned Numbers Authority (IANA). It was signed on March 1, 2000 and ratified by the ICANN Board on March 10, 2000.

The MoU's intent is exclusively to define the technical work IANA does on behalf of the IETF and the Internet Research Task Force (IRTF). ICANN may provide similar services to others for protocols outside the IETF's scope, and nothing in the MoU limits that. It stays in effect until changed or cancelled by mutual consent, or cancelled by either party with at least six months notice.
sections.eli5: Two groups wrote down their deal about the people who keep the Internet's lists. Either one can end the deal if it gives six months warning.

sections.title: The Parties and Terms
sections.content:
The MoU defines its players. IANA is a traditional name for the technical team that makes and publishes assignments of Internet protocol technical parameters, and that team is now part of ICANN. The IAB is an oversight committee of the IETF and is chartered to designate the IANA on behalf of the IETF. The IESG is a management committee of the IETF. The IRTF is overseen by the IAB, and the IRSG manages it.

It also defines the RFC series as the archival document series of the IETF, also used by the IRTF and by third parties, and ISOC as the not-for-profit corporation that supports the IETF.
sections.eli5: Before the rules, the MoU says who everyone is: the team that keeps the lists, the committee that picks them, and the group that manages the rules.

sections.title: How IANA Assigns Parameters
sections.content:
For protocols within the IETF's scope, ICANN agrees to make IANA follow the requirements in Section 4. IANA assigns and registers protocol parameters only as directed by the criteria and procedures in RFCs, including Proposed, Draft and full Internet Standards, Best Current Practice documents and any other RFC that calls for an IANA assignment. Where nothing is specified, or the text is ambiguous, IANA continues past and current practice unless the IESG directs otherwise.

In doubt or in a technical dispute, IANA seeks and follows technical guidance exclusively from the IESG, which may appoint an expert. IANA works with the IETF to develop missing criteria over time and adopts them when the IESG instructs it. If IANA and the IESG disagree technically, both seek guidance from the IAB, whose decision is final.

Domain names and IP address blocks raise policy issues beyond technical ones, and those policy issues are outside the scope of the MoU. Technical uses (such as domain names for inverse DNS lookup), specialised address blocks (such as multicast or anycast) and experimental assignments stay under Section 4.
sections.eli5: The rule book says: hand out numbers exactly as the written rules say. If the rules are unclear, ask the IESG. If there is still an argument, the IAB decides.

sections.title: Service Duties and Appeals
sections.content:
IANA must make information about each current assignment, including contact details for the assignee, available to the public on-line and free of charge. Assignments published in RFCs by the RFC Editor count as meeting this requirement.

IANA must provide on-line facilities for requesting assignments and either carry them out or deny them for non-conformance with technical requirements, in a timely manner. There is no charge without the consent of the IAB, and requests may be denied only on legitimate technical grounds. For protocols in the IETF's scope, denials can be appealed to the IESG and then the IAB.

IANA has non-voting liaison seats on appropriate IETF committees and reviews all documents in IETF Last Call, raising any issues of concern with the IESG. For parameters relevant to the IRTF, the IRTF and IRSG take the place of the IETF and IESG, and the IAB decides any question over which applies.
sections.eli5: The list keepers must show the lists to everyone for free, answer requests quickly, and only say no for good technical reasons. If someone is told no, they can ask a higher group to look again.

sections.title: Legal Terms and Effect
sections.content:
The general terms say the MoU does not make any party a partner, joint venturer, agent, principal or franchisee of another. No party may transfer its rights or obligations without the written consent of the other parties. The agreement needed approval or ratification by the ICANN Board of Directors, and ICANN's signatory was to use best efforts to deliver it within two months of signing.

If ICANN adopts a policy that prevents it from complying with Section 4 for technical domain names, specialised address blocks or experimental assignments, it must notify the IETF, which may then cancel the MoU. The RFC's security considerations say the document does not directly impact the security of the Internet.
sections.eli5: The deal does not make the two groups business partners. If one group starts breaking the rules, the other can walk away.
